title: Base-Parametrized Digital Root dr_b(n)
description: Generalizes the digital root from base 10 to arbitrary base b ≥ 2. Proves the closed-form formula dr_b(n) = 1 + ((n-1) mod (b-1)), idempotence, divisibility criteria, multiplicativity, and specializations to base 10 (casting out nines) and base 2.

originalContributions: Base-parametrized digital root definition and closed form (proved)
Range, fixed point, and idempotence properties (proved)
Divisibility by (b-1) and factor divisibility rule (proved)
Concrete examples in hex (base 16), octal (base 8), and base 7 (proved)

openQuestion: Can Lean 4 formalize a base-parametrized version of the digital root, generalizing the base-10 results to arbitrary base b?
significance: This formalization reveals the universal algebraic structure behind digital roots: for any base b ≥ 3, the digital root dr_b(n) depends only on n mod (b-1), because b ≡ 1 (mod b-1). This single congruence explains casting out nines (b=10), casting out sevens in octal (b=8), and every other base's analog. The formalization uses Mathlib's Nat.modEq_digits_sum as the bridge between digit sums and modular arithmetic.

overview.historicalContext:
The digital root -- the single digit obtained by repeatedly summing a number's digits -- has been used as a divisibility check since at least the 12th century, when it appeared in Fibonacci's *Liber Abaci* (1202) under the name *casting out nines*. The technique was known to Arabic and Indian mathematicians even earlier; al-Khwarizmi described it in his 9th-century treatise on Hindu-Arabic numerals.

The generalization to arbitrary bases reveals that the digital root is not a peculiarity of base 10, but a consequence of the fundamental fact that $b \equiv 1 \pmod{b-1}$ for any base $b$. This means $b^k \equiv 1 \pmod{b-1}$, so $n = \sum_i d_i b^i \equiv \sum_i d_i \pmod{b-1}$ -- the digit sum preserves residues modulo $b-1$.

The closed-form formula $\text{dr}_b(n) = 1 + ((n-1) \bmod (b-1))$ for $n > 0$ was known informally but rarely stated precisely. It maps $\{1, 2, \ldots, b-1\}$ cyclically through the residues, with the adjustment ensuring $\text{dr}_b(b-1) = b-1$ rather than 0.

In computer science, the digital root in base $2^k$ (binary, hex, octal) is computed by simple bitmasking, and the factor divisibility rule explains why casting out 15s works in hexadecimal and casting out 7s works in octal -- both are instances of the general principle that divisors of $b-1$ can be tested via digit sums.
overview.problemStatement:
**Definition**: For base $b \geq 2$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$:
$$\text{dr}_b(n) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } n = 0 \\ 1 + ((n-1) \bmod (b-1)) & \text{if } n > 0 \end{cases}$$

**Prove**:
1. Range: $1 \leq \text{dr}_b(n) \leq b-1$ for $n > 0$
2. Fixed point: $\text{dr}_b(n) = n$ for $1 \leq n \leq b-1$
3. Idempotence: $\text{dr}_b(\text{dr}_b(n)) = \text{dr}_b(n)$
4. Congruence: $n \equiv \text{dr}_b(n) \pmod{b-1}$
5. Divisibility: $(b-1) \mid n \iff \text{dr}_b(n) = b-1$ (for $n > 0$)
6. Factor rule: $d \mid (b-1) \Rightarrow (d \mid n \iff d \mid \text{digitSum}_b(n))$
overview.proofStrategy:
The formalization takes a **definition-first** approach: define $\text{dr}_b(n)$ directly via the closed form, then derive all properties from modular arithmetic.

**Key lemma**: For $b \geq 3$, $b \bmod (b-1) = 1$. This is proved by rewriting $b = (b-1) + 1$ and applying `Nat.mod_eq_sub_mod`.

**Congruence**: To show $n \equiv \text{dr}_b(n) \pmod{b-1}$, write $n = (n-1) + 1$ and compute both sides modulo $b-1$. The LHS gives $((n-1) \bmod (b-1)) + 1 \bmod (b-1)$; the RHS gives the same by definition of $\text{dr}_b$.

**Idempotence**: Since $1 \leq \text{dr}_b(n) \leq b-1$ (range), it is a single-digit number, so $\text{dr}_b(\text{dr}_b(n)) = \text{dr}_b(n)$ by the fixed-point property.

**Divisibility bridge**: Uses Mathlib's `Nat.modEq_digits_sum` to connect $n \equiv \text{digitSum}_b(n) \pmod{b-1}$, then combines with the congruence of $\text{dr}_b$ to establish divisibility criteria.
keyInsights: The entire theory rests on one fact: $b \equiv 1 \pmod{b-1}$. This single congruence implies $b^k \equiv 1 \pmod{b-1}$, so $n = \sum d_i b^i \equiv \sum d_i \pmod{b-1}$ -- the digit sum preserves residues mod $b-1$.
The closed-form formula $\text{dr}_b(n) = 1 + ((n-1) \bmod (b-1))$ avoids iterative digit manipulation entirely. All properties reduce to `omega` or `Nat.mod_lt` -- no recursion, no digit sequences.

Idempotence follows automatically from the range bound: since $\text{dr}_b(n) \in \{1, \ldots, b-1\}$, it is already a single-digit fixed point. This is a clean example of how range analysis implies algebraic properties.

The factor divisibility rule generalizes casting out nines: for any $d \mid (b-1)$, we have $d \mid n \iff d \mid \text{digitSum}_b(n)$. In base 10, this gives divisibility by 3 and 9; in base 16, by 3, 5, and 15; in base 12, by 11.
Base 2 is degenerate: $b - 1 = 1$, so $\text{dr}_2(n) = 1$ for all $n > 0$. Every positive integer has digital root 1 in binary, because $1 \mid n$ for all $n$.

sections.title: Key Helper: b mod (b-1) = 1
sections.summary: Proves the foundational congruence $b \bmod (b-1) = 1$ for $b \geq 3$. Uses `Nat.mod_eq_sub_mod` to rewrite $b \bmod (b-1) = (b - (b-1)) \bmod (b-1) = 1 \bmod (b-1) = 1$.
sections.mathContext: $b = (b-1) + 1 \Rightarrow b \bmod (b-1) = 1$. This is the algebraic reason that digit sums preserve residues: $b^k \equiv 1^k = 1 \pmod{b-1}$.

sections.title: The Digital Root Definition
sections.summary: Defines `digitalRootBase b n` via the closed form: 0 for $n = 0$, $1 + ((n-1) \bmod (b-1))$ for $n > 0$. Two basic lemmas: the zero case and the positive case.

sections.title: Core Congruence Property
sections.summary: Proves two congruence results: (1) Mathlib's `Nat.modEq_digits_sum` gives $n \equiv \text{digitSum}_b(n) \pmod{b-1}$, and (2) $n \equiv \text{dr}_b(n) \pmod{b-1}$ by direct computation. The second proof rewrites $n = (n-1) + 1$ and uses `Nat.add_mod`.

sections.title: Range, Fixed Points, and Idempotence
sections.summary: Three structural properties: (1) **Range**: $1 \leq \text{dr}_b(n) \leq b-1$ for $n > 0$, using `Nat.mod_lt`. (2) **Fixed point**: $\text{dr}_b(n) = n$ for $1 \leq n \leq b-1$, using `Nat.mod_eq_of_lt`. (3) **Idempotence**: $\text{dr}_b(\text{dr}_b(n)) = \text{dr}_b(n)$, composing range with fixed point.
sections.mathContext: $\text{dr}_b$ is a retraction onto $\{1, \ldots, b-1\}$ (with 0 mapped to 0). Idempotence ($\text{dr}_b^2 = \text{dr}_b$) makes it a projection.

sections.title: Divisibility Criteria
sections.summary: Three divisibility results: (1) $(b-1) \mid n \iff \text{dr}_b(n) = b-1$ for $n > 0$, proved by case analysis on $n = k(b-1)$ and using the congruence property. (2) $(b-1) \mid n \iff (b-1) \mid \text{digitSum}_b(n)$, directly from Mathlib's `dvd_iff_dvd_digits_sum`. (3) The **factor divisibility rule**: for any $d \mid (b-1)$, $d \mid n \iff d \mid \text{digitSum}_b(n)$.
sections.mathContext: General divisibility rule: if $d \mid (b-1)$ and $d \geq 2$, then $d \mid n \iff d \mid \sum_i d_i$ where $n = \sum_i d_i b^i$. Special cases: $3 \mid n \iff 3 \mid \text{digitSum}_{10}(n)$; $7 \mid n \iff 7 \mid \text{digitSum}_8(n)$.

sections.title: Base-10 Specialization and Concrete Examples
sections.summary: Shows the base-10 digital root is a special case ($b = 10$), then verifies concrete examples in hexadecimal (base 16: $\text{dr}_{16}(15) = 15$, $\text{dr}_{16}(255) = 15$), octal (base 8: $\text{dr}_8(64) = 1$), and base 7 ($\text{dr}_7(42) = 6$). All computed via `native_decide`.

conclusion.summary: This formalization demonstrates that digital roots are a universal phenomenon governed by a single algebraic fact: $b \equiv 1 \pmod{b-1}$. By defining $\text{dr}_b$ via its closed form rather than iterative digit summation, all properties reduce to elementary modular arithmetic. The factor divisibility rule subsumes every classical digit-sum test (casting out nines, divisibility by 3, etc.) as special cases.
conclusion.implications:
**Number Theory**: The digital root is a retraction from $\mathbb{N}$ onto $\{0, 1, \ldots, b-1\}$ that preserves residues modulo $b-1$. Its idempotence makes it a canonical representative of congruence classes.

**Computer Science**: In base $2^k$, the digital root can be computed by bitwise AND: $\text{dr}_{2^k}(n) = 1 + ((n-1) \& (2^k - 2))$, giving O(1) divisibility tests for factors of $2^k - 1$.

**Pedagogy**: The base-parametrized formulation reveals *why* casting out nines works -- not because 9 is special, but because 10 - 1 = 9. Students in octal cast out 7s, students in hex cast out 15s, by the same universal principle.
openQuestions: Formalize the iterative definition of the digital root (repeatedly sum digits until a single digit remains) and prove it equals the closed form $1 + ((n-1) \bmod (b-1))$.
Extend to the generalized digital root in mixed-radix systems (e.g., time: base 60 seconds, base 60 minutes, base 24 hours).
Prove that the digital root function is the unique function $f : \mathbb{N} \to \{0, \ldots, b-1\}$ satisfying $f(n) \equiv n \pmod{b-1}$, $f(0) = 0$, and $f(n) \neq 0$ for $n > 0$.
Connect to Niven numbers: $n$ is a Niven number in base $b$ if $\text{digitSum}_b(n) \mid n$. Formalize the density of Niven numbers and its dependence on the base.
